title: Sum a Vector Without Overflowing
statement:
`std::vector<int>` is the workhorse container for "a resizable list of
numbers" in C++, and passing one to a function almost always means passing
it `const&` -- a read-only reference -- rather than by value: taking it by
value would copy every element just to read them, for no benefit, every
single time the function is called.

## Your function

```
long long SumVector(const std::vector<int>& values);
```

Return the sum of every element of `values`. `values` may be empty, in
which case the sum is `0`.

## Watch out

- **The return type is `long long`, not `int`.** `values` can hold enough
  large `int` elements that their true sum does not fit in 32 bits, even
  though every individual element does. Accumulate into the `long long`
  the return type already commits you to from the very first addition --
  not into an `int` total you only widen at the end, by which point an
  overflow has already happened and wrapped to a nonsense negative number.
- **`const&` means you cannot modify `values`.** The compiler enforces
  this -- assigning to `values[i]` or calling a mutating method will not
  compile -- which is the point: this function only ever needs to read the
  vector, and the signature says so.
- An empty vector's sum is `0`, not an error and not a value that needs a
  special check: a loop that simply never executes its body already
  produces the right answer.

tests.name: an empty vector sums to zero
a sum that overflows a 32-bit int but not a 64-bit long long
tests.description: 6,000,000,000 is past INT_MAX (~2.1 billion) -- accumulating into a 32-bit int wraps to a negative number.
